patient.name: Maureen Doyle
patient.setting: Respiratory clinic, then admission to the respiratory ward
patient.complaint: Swollen ankles and breathlessness getting worse over 3 months
background: One fall last month after climbing stairs to her flat
Takes tiotropium and a combination inhaler

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with COPD plus raised JVP, ankle oedema and a loud P2 (cor pulmonale), or a young woman with exertional syncope. You may be asked for the ECG or auscultation finding.

points: Breathless walking to the kitchen, worse over 3 months.
Ankles so swollen her shoes no longer fit.
She blacked out briefly **climbing the stairs**.

steps.lead: Maureen's long-standing **COPD** is the commonest kind of cause: chronic lung disease raising her pulmonary artery pressure until the right heart strains.

points: **JVP raised** to 7 cm; pitting oedema to the knees.
Loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area: **loud P2**.
Left parasternal heave; tender, enlarged liver.
Chest: quiet breath sounds, no crackles.

steps.lead: Exertional **syncope**, fatigue and breathlessness with a raised JVP, oedema and **loud P2**: Maureen has the signs of a pressure-loaded right heart.

steps.q: COPD, raised JVP, ankle oedema, loud P2, clear lung bases. What is this?
steps.r: Right heart failure from long-standing lung disease is **cor pulmonale**. LVF gives bibasal crackles; nephrotic syndrome has no raised JVP.

steps.lead: Maureen is the textbook signature: **cor pulmonale** from COPD. Her ECG will be checked for **P pulmonale**.

visual.title: Maureen's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with T inversion V1 to V3 (right ventricular strain). Look for tall, peaked P waves in II: P pulmonale.

steps.lead: Maureen's blackout on the stairs is exertional **syncope**: the strained right ventricle cannot raise output on effort. Arrhythmias are the other danger.
Maureen has no bronchiectasis and is past childbearing age, but in a young woman **idiopathic PAH** can flare dangerously in **pregnancy**.

steps.text: Ankle oedema plus breathlessness is not always left heart failure. **Clear lung bases, raised JVP and loud P2** in a COPD patient point to the **right** heart.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (echocardiogram) or 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (right heart catheterisation).

steps.title: Admission bloods and gas
steps.text: Chronic hypoxia (and secondary polycythaemia) drives the pressure; high BNP reflects ventricular stretch.

steps.q: Which test should come first to look for pulmonary hypertension?
steps.r: **Echocardiogram** is the initial investigation: it estimates pulmonary pressure and shows the right ventricle. Catheterisation confirms it.

steps.lead: Maureen has an **echo** first, with an ECG, a chest X-ray and, to look for clots, a CT pulmonary angiogram as supporting tests.

visual.title: Maureen's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged proximal pulmonary arteries at both hila and a large heart from right-sided enlargement; lungs hyperinflated from COPD.

points: Echo: **dilated, thick right ventricle**; flattened septum.
Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure **62 mmHg**.

steps.lead: To confirm, Maureen has **right heart catheterisation**, which measures the pressures directly: the gold standard.

visual.title: Mean pulmonary artery pressure at catheterisation
visual.label: Maureen 38
visual.caption: ESC/ERS 2022 defines PH as resting mean PAP above 20 mmHg at right heart catheterisation.

steps.text: **Initial** = echocardiogram. **Diagnostic / gold standard** = right heart catheterisation. Read the lead-in carefully.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (oxygen and diuretics in cor pulmonale), PAH-specific drugs (vasodilators, endothelin receptor antagonists, anticoagulation), and transplant for severe disease.

points: Maureen: hypoxic (PaO2 7.1 kPa) and fluid overloaded.
Weight up 6 kg; oedema to the knees.

steps.q: What is the most appropriate initial management for Maureen?
steps.r: Pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure: **oxygen** for hypoxia and **diuretics** for overload first. Vasodilators are for PAH.

steps.lead: Maureen gets **controlled oxygen** (she is hypoxic) and **furosemide** (she is overloaded), the first-line supportive treatment.

visual.title: Maureen on furosemide
visual.caption: 6 kg of fluid off in a week as the oedema settles.

steps.lead: The real driver is Maureen's **COPD**, so optimising it (and long-term oxygen for her chronic hypoxia) is the long-term plan.
If Maureen had **pulmonary arterial hypertension** (for example idiopathic), a specialist centre would add **vasodilators**, **endothelin receptor antagonists** and **anticoagulation**.

steps.title: Managing pulmonary hypertension
nodes: Treat the cause: lung disease, clots, left heart
Severe or refractory → lung transplant referral

steps.lead: If her disease became **severe** despite all this and she was fit enough, referral for **lung transplantation** would be considered.

steps.text: Do not reach for sildenafil or bosentan in COPD cor pulmonale. Pulmonary vasodilators are for **PAH**; lung-disease PH is treated through **oxygen and the lung disease**.

steps.lead: Maureen's diagnosis (mean PAP >20 mmHg at catheterisation) and treatment follow the **ESC/ERS** pulmonary hypertension guidelines.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why COPD raises pulmonary pressure (hypoxic vasoconstriction), why the right heart fails, how unresolved clots cause it, and how vasodilators work.

steps.lead: Maureen's alveoli are hypoxic, so her lung arteries **constrict**. Years of this **remodel** the vessel wall, fixing the resistance high.

steps.title: From COPD to swollen ankles
nodes: RV afterload rises: hypertrophy then failure

steps.lead: Maureen's right ventricle first **thickened** against the pressure, then **dilated and failed**: that is her raised JVP, oedema and big liver.

steps.q: Why does Maureen have a loud P2?
o: Pulmonary valve closes against high pressure
steps.r: High pulmonary artery pressure **slams the pulmonary valve shut**, making the pulmonary component of S2 loud.

steps.lead: Maureen's CTPA showed no clots, but **unresolved emboli** that scar and block the vessels are another way resistance climbs.
PAH drugs such as **PDE-5 inhibitors** and **prostacyclin analogues** relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle to lower resistance; they would not fix Maureen's hypoxic remodelling.

steps.text: Pressure overload = **afterload**. The RV is thin-walled and copes poorly, so sustained pulmonary hypertension ends in **cor pulmonale**.

o: Right heart failure from long-standing lung disease
mcq.r: Right-sided heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary disease such as COPD.

mcq.q: Which ECG change is characteristic of pulmonary hypertension?
mcq.r: Tall, peaked P waves (P pulmonale) from right atrial enlargement.

mcq.q: Which heart sound finding suggests pulmonary hypertension?
mcq.r: Split S2 with a loud pulmonary component.

mcq.q: What is the initial investigation for suspected pulmonary hypertension?
What is the gold-standard investigation for pulmonary hypertension?
mcq.r: Right heart catheterisation measures pulmonary pressures directly.

mcq.q: First-line management of pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure?
mcq.r: Oxygen if hypoxic, diuretics if fluid overloaded.

mcq.q: Which drug class is used specifically in pulmonary arterial hypertension?
mcq.r: PAH: vasodilators, endothelin receptor antagonists and anticoagulation.

mcq.q: Why does COPD raise pulmonary artery pressure?
mcq.r: Hypoxic vasoconstriction then vascular remodelling raise resistance.

mcq.q: Why does the right ventricle fail in pulmonary hypertension?
mcq.r: Raised pulmonary pressure increases RV afterload: hypertrophy, dilatation, failure.

prompts.q: What is pulmonary hypertension and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lungs, clots, heart, or idiopathic.

points.p: Raised pulmonary arterial pressure causing right heart strain and failure
points.why: Mean PAP above 20 mmHg at rest (ESC/ERS 2022).

points.p: Chronic lung disease: COPD, interstitial lung disease
points.why: Lung disease is a very common cause.

points.p: PE / chronic thromboembolic disease
points.why: Unresolved emboli block the vasculature.

points.p: Left heart disease and congenital heart disease
points.why: Left heart disease raises pressure backwards.

points.p: Idiopathic (rare)
points.why: Think of a young woman with exertional syncope.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and signs of pulmonary hypertension?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: exertional syncope plus right heart signs.

points.p: Breathlessness, fatigue, chest pain, progressive symptoms
points.why: Non-specific, so it is often diagnosed late.

points.p: Exertional syncope
points.why: The RV cannot raise output on effort.

points.p: Raised JVP and pitting oedema (right heart failure, late)
points.why: Right heart failure is a late sign.

points.p: Split S2 with loud P2
points.why: The pulmonary valve closes against high pressure.

points.p: Early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation
points.why: The dilated pulmonary valve ring leaks.

prompts.q: What is cor pulmonale and what does the ECG show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: COPD plus right heart failure.

points.p: Right-sided heart failure from long-standing lung disease (e.g. COPD)
points.why: Lung bases stay clear, unlike left heart failure.

points.p: ECG: P pulmonale (tall, peaked P waves)
points.why: Right atrial enlargement; do not confuse with P mitrale (bifid).

prompts.q: What complications and associations of pulmonary hypertension should you know?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what kills, and what makes it worse.

points.p: Right heart failure
points.why: The end point of sustained high afterload.

points.p: Syncope and arrhythmias
points.why: Arrhythmias can cause sudden death.

points.p: Associated with bronchiectasis
points.why: Chronic lung disease and hypoxia.

points.p: Idiopathic PAH exacerbated by pregnancy
points.why: Pregnancy carries high mortality in PAH.

points.p: Initial: echocardiogram
points.why: Estimates pressure and shows RV size.

points.p: Gold standard: right heart catheterisation
points.why: Measures the pressures directly.

points.p: Supporting: ECG, chest X-ray, CT pulmonary angiography
points.why: CTPA looks for thromboembolic disease.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: supportive, then PAH drugs, then transplant, always the cause.

points.p: With right heart failure: oxygen (if hypoxic) and diuretics (if overloaded)
points.why: First-line supportive treatment.

points.p: Pulmonary vasodilators
points.why: Second-line, mainly for PAH.

points.p: PAH: anticoagulation and endothelin receptor antagonists
points.why: Bosentan is the classic ERA.

points.p: Severe: lung transplantation
points.why: For severe or refractory disease.

points.p: Always treat the underlying cause
points.why: Lung disease or thromboembolism.

prompts.q: Why does chronic lung disease raise pulmonary pressure and the right heart fail?

points.p: Sustained hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
points.why: Unique to the lung: low oxygen narrows its arteries.

points.p: Remodelling: medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis, raising resistance
points.why: Makes the rise fixed.

points.p: Raised RV afterload: hypertrophy, dilatation, failure
points.why: Gives raised JVP, oedema and hepatomegaly.

prompts.q: How do thromboembolism and PAH drugs affect pulmonary vascular resistance?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: blockage up, relaxation down.

points.p: Unresolved emboli obstruct the vasculature, raising resistance
points.why: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

points.p: Vasodilators (PDE-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues) relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle
points.why: Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor.

points.p: Endothelin receptor antagonists block endothelin, a vasoconstrictor
points.why: Endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor and mitogen.

glossary.Pulmonary hypertension: Raised blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries; mean pressure above 20 mmHg at rest.
glossary.PAH: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: disease of the small lung arteries themselves, such as idiopathic PAH.
glossary.Idiopathic PAH: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with no identifiable cause; rare, often young women.
glossary.Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by long-standing lung disease such as COPD.
glossary.P pulmonale: Tall, peaked P waves (over 2.5 mm in II) from right atrial enlargement.
glossary.P mitrale: Broad, notched P waves from left atrial enlargement, as in mitral stenosis.
glossary.P2: The pulmonary valve component of the second heart sound; loud in pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.Split S2: Second heart sound heard as two parts, aortic then pulmonary closure.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure: height of the venous pulse in the neck, reflecting right atrial pressure.
glossary.Parasternal heave: Lifting felt at the left sternal edge from an enlarged right ventricle.
glossary.Pitting oedema: Swelling that keeps a dent after pressing, from fluid in the tissues.
glossary.Hepatomegaly: Enlarged liver; in right heart failure it is congested and may be tender.
glossary.Early diastolic murmur: Murmur just after S2; here from pulmonary regurgitation (Graham Steell murmur).
glossary.Pulmonary regurgitation: Backflow through the pulmonary valve, often because the dilated artery stretches the valve ring.
glossary.Exertional syncope: Fainting during effort because cardiac output cannot rise to meet demand.
glossary.Echocardiogram: Ultrasound of the heart; estimates pulmonary pressure and shows the right ventricle.
glossary.Right heart catheterisation: A catheter passed into the right heart and pulmonary artery to measure pressures directly; the gold standard.
glossary.mPAP: Mean pulmonary artery pressure; above 20 mmHg at rest defines pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.CTPA: CT pulmonary angiogram: contrast CT showing clots in the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.NT-proBNP: A blood marker released when heart muscle is stretched; raised in heart failure and right heart strain.
glossary.RV afterload: The resistance the right ventricle pumps against, set mainly by pulmonary vascular resistance.
glossary.Pulmonary vascular resistance: How hard it is for blood to flow through the lung vessels.
glossary.Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: Narrowing of lung arteries in response to low alveolar oxygen.
glossary.Medial hypertrophy: Thickening of the muscle layer of an artery wall.
glossary.Intimal fibrosis: Scarring of the inner lining of an artery, narrowing it.
glossary.Remodelling: Permanent structural change in vessel walls that fixes resistance high.
glossary.Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hyperte: Pulmonary hypertension from unresolved clots scarring and blocking the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.CTEPH: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, caused by unresolved pulmonary emboli.
glossary.Pulmonary vasodilators: Drugs that relax lung artery smooth muscle to lower pulmonary pressure, used in PAH.
glossary.Endothelin receptor antagonist: Drug, such as bosentan, that blocks the vasoconstrictor endothelin in PAH.
glossary.Bosentan: An oral endothelin receptor antagonist used in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
glossary.PDE-5 inhibitor: Drug such as sildenafil that boosts nitric oxide signalling to relax pulmonary arteries.
glossary.Sildenafil: A PDE-5 inhibitor used as a pulmonary vasodilator in PAH.
glossary.Prostacyclin analogue: Drug mimicking prostacyclin, a natural vasodilator, used in PAH (e.g. epoprostenol).
glossary.Bronchiectasis: Permanently widened, scarred airways with chronic productive cough; associated with pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: smoking-related fixed airflow obstruction.
glossary.Long-term oxygen therapy: Oxygen for at least 15 hours a day for chronic hypoxia, which slows pulmonary hypertension in COPD.
glossary.Secondary polycythaemia: Raised red cell count driven by chronic hypoxia raising erythropoietin.
glossary.ESC/ERS: European Society of Cardiology and European Respiratory Society, who publish the pulmonary hypertension guidelines.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man with severe COPD has 2 months of worsening breathlessness and ankle swelling. His JVP is raised 6 cm, there is pitting oedema to the knees and a loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area. His chest has reduced breath sounds without crackles. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: why does a COPD patient have oedema?

clues: loud second heart sound in the pulmonary area
steps.x: Right heart failure signs plus loud P2, with clear bases, in chronic lung disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right heart failure from lung disease: **cor pulmonale**.

elim: Albumin is normal and there is no proteinuria.
No fever, sputum change or acute history; this is 2 months of right heart failure.
LVF would give bibasal crackles, not clear lungs and a loud P2.
SVCO swells the face and arms with a fixed, non-pulsatile JVP, not leg oedema.

steps.x: **A. Cor pulmonale.** Rule: COPD + raised JVP + oedema + loud P2 = right heart failure from PH.

technique.stem: A 36 year old woman has 9 months of progressive breathlessness and two episodes of fainting while running for a bus. She has a loud P2 and a left parasternal heave. An echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle with an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 70 mmHg and a normal left ventricle. A CT pulmonary angiogram shows no emboli.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic': the gold standard, not the first test.

clues: fainting while running for a bus
estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 70 mmHg
steps.x: Echo already suggests PH; clots excluded; no lung disease: likely idiopathic PAH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm by measuring pressures directly: **right heart catheterisation**.

elim: Cardiac MRI shows RV structure but does not measure pulmonary pressure directly.
CT coronary angiogram looks for coronary disease.
Exercise testing is unsafe with exertional syncope and does not diagnose PH.
TOE gives no better pressure estimate than transthoracic echo.

steps.x: **D. Right heart catheterisation.** Rule: echo first, catheter confirms.

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman with COPD is admitted with worsening ankle swelling and breathlessness. She has a raised JVP, pitting oedema to the thighs and a loud P2. Echocardiogram confirms pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular dilatation and a normal left ventricle. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 85% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of PH with right heart failure.
Fluid overloaded and hypoxic, with lung-disease PH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oxygen** for hypoxia and **diuretics** for overload.

elim: Endothelin receptor antagonists are for PAH, not COPD-related PH.
Digoxin is not first-line here.
Transplant is for severe refractory disease, not initial care.
Pulmonary vasodilators are for PAH and can worsen gas exchange in COPD.

steps.x: **C. Furosemide with controlled oxygen.** Controlled, because her CO2 is raised.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with long-standing COPD has bilateral ankle oedema, a raised JVP and a tender enlarged liver. His lung bases are clear. Echocardiogram shows a hypertrophied, dilated right ventricle and normal left ventricular function. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his ankle oedema?

steps.x: Mechanism of oedema in cor pulmonale.
Right ventricle thickened then dilated against high pulmonary pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pulmonary hypertension raises **RV afterload**; the RV fails and venous pressure backs up.

elim: Low albumin would not raise the JVP.
LV function is normal and lung bases are clear.
Lymphatic obstruction does not raise JVP or enlarge the liver.
Varicose valve failure is local and does not explain the JVP or liver.

steps.x: **B. Increased RV afterload.** Hypertrophy, then dilatation, then failure.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has 1 year of progressive breathlessness and fainted twice while climbing stairs. She has no lung disease and has never smoked. There is a loud P2 and a left parasternal heave. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged proximal pulmonary arteries and an enlarged cardiac silhouette; clear lung fields.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Exertional syncope, loud P2, RV heave and enlarged pulmonary arteries in a young woman with no lung disease is idiopathic PAH. Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a young woman with exertional syncope.
Right-sided pressure overload with no lung cause; X-ray shows big pulmonary arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Idiopathic PAH.**

elim: Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur and is rare at 32.
HCM gives an ejection systolic murmur and LV, not RV, signs.
Vasovagal syncope has triggers and no cardiac signs.
WPW causes palpitations; the ECG would show delta waves.

steps.x: **C. Idiopathic PAH.** Young woman + exertional syncope + loud P2.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with COPD has ankle oedema, a raised JVP and a loud P2. Echocardiogram shows right atrial and right ventricular enlargement. His pulse rate is 90 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
o: Short PR interval with delta waves
practice.e: Right atrial enlargement from pulmonary hypertension gives tall, peaked P waves: P pulmonale. P mitrale is bifid P waves from left atrial enlargement.

steps.x: ECG finding in cor pulmonale.

clues: right atrial and right ventricular enlargement
steps.x: Right-sided enlargement from PH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Big right atrium: **P pulmonale**.

elim: P mitrale is left atrial enlargement.
Peaked T waves mean hyperkalaemia.
Delta waves are WPW.
Saddle ST elevation is pericarditis.

steps.x: **B. P pulmonale.** Tall P waves in II.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has 6 months of increasing breathlessness and fatigue. She has had two pulmonary emboli in the past. Her JVP is raised and she has mild ankle oedema. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of the heart?
o: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Fourth heart sound at the apex
Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
practice.e: Pulmonary hypertension makes the pulmonary valve close forcefully: a split S2 with a loud P2.

steps.x: Heart sound in suspected pulmonary hypertension.

clues: two pulmonary emboli in the past
steps.x: Recurrent PEs and right heart signs: pulmonary hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Loud P2.**

elim: Mid-diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis.
Ejection systolic to the carotids is aortic stenosis.
An S4 at the apex reflects a stiff left ventricle.
Pansystolic to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.

steps.x: **D. Loud P2.**

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had a pulmonary embolism 18 months ago and took anticoagulation for 3 months. He now has progressive breathlessness on exertion and nearly fainted walking uphill. Echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle with high estimated pulmonary pressure. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Unresolved emboli obstruct the pulmonary vessels, raising resistance: chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Hb is normal, so not anaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis after a previous PE.
Slow, progressive right heart strain after PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.**

elim: Haemoglobin is normal.
Asthma does not dilate the right ventricle.
Hyperventilation has normal echo and saturations.
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble and a big left atrium.

steps.x: **E. Thromboembolic PH.** Previous PE + progressive breathlessness + RV strain.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman with known idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension is 26 weeks pregnant. Over 2 weeks she has become more breathless with swollen ankles and abdominal discomfort. Her JVP is raised 8 cm and she has a tender enlarged liver. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: Pregnancy exacerbates idiopathic PAH, and the overloaded RV fails: raised JVP, oedema and a congested liver. No hypertension or proteinuria, so not pre-eclampsia.

steps.x: What is the complication here?
Pregnancy worsens PAH; congestive right-sided signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right heart failure** from worsening PAH.

elim: No wheeze, and asthma does not raise the JVP.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy appears in the last month or after delivery and is LV failure.
BP is normal and there is no proteinuria.
UTI does not cause a raised JVP or hepatomegaly.

steps.x: **D. Right heart failure.** Pregnancy is a classic trigger in PAH.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) has worsening ankle oedema and a loud P2. She has never had a venous thromboembolism. Echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle and a normal left ventricle and valves. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her pulmonary hypertension?
practice.e: Severe COPD with chronic hypoxia causes hypoxic vasoconstriction and remodelling: pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease, leading to cor pulmonale.

steps.x: Cause of pulmonary hypertension.
Hypoxic lung disease; clots and left heart excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **COPD**: chronic lung disease.

elim: No history of venous thromboembolism.
No congenital lesion on echo, and she presents at 69.
Idiopathic is rare and a diagnosis of exclusion; COPD is an obvious cause.
The LV and valves are normal.

steps.x: **A. COPD.** Find the cause in the history.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with interstitial lung disease has increasing breathlessness, ankle oedema and a loud P2. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. His ECG shows tall P waves in lead II.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Echocardiogram is the initial investigation for suspected pulmonary hypertension; right heart catheterisation confirms it.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation.

clues: tall P waves in lead II
steps.x: Suspected PH from lung disease, with P pulmonale.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Echocardiogram.**

elim: Cardiac MRI is not first-line.
CTPA is a supporting test for clots, not the first test.
Catheterisation is the gold standard, after echo.
Spirometry assesses the lung disease, not the pressure.

steps.x: **C. Echocardiogram.**

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman is being investigated for suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension. She has exertional breathlessness and a loud P2. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
o: Enlarged pulmonary arteries on chest X-ray
Estimated systolic pressure of 58 mmHg on echocardiogram
Mean pulmonary artery pressure of 36 mmHg at catheterisation
practice.e: Right heart catheterisation measures pulmonary pressure directly and is the gold standard. Echo only estimates it.

steps.x: Which result is diagnostic?
One result comes from the gold-standard test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Catheterisation-measured mean PAP.**

elim: BNP is non-specific heart strain.
X-ray changes support but do not confirm.
Echo estimates, it does not measure directly.
P pulmonale supports but does not confirm.

steps.x: **D. Mean PAP at catheterisation.** Gold standard.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman has chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after recurrent pulmonary emboli. She is breathless on climbing one flight of stairs. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. She has no ankle oedema.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Always treat the underlying cause: here thromboembolism, so lifelong anticoagulation. Thrombolysis is for acute massive PE.

steps.x: Long-term management.
Cause is clots; not overloaded, so no diuretic needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the cause: **anticoagulation**.

elim: Aspirin does not prevent venous thromboembolism adequately.
No obstructive airway disease.
Steroids do not treat thromboembolic disease.
Thrombolysis is for acute massive PE, not chronic disease.

steps.x: **B. Lifelong anticoagulation.**

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension confirmed on right heart catheterisation. She has no oedema and her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She is reviewed at a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug class to start?
practice.e: PAH is treated with pulmonary vasodilators, endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g. bosentan) and anticoagulation. She is not hypoxic or overloaded, so oxygen and diuretics are not needed.

steps.x: Drug class for confirmed PAH.
True PAH, without overload or hypoxia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Endothelin receptor antagonist** (with vasodilators and anticoagulation).

elim: ACE inhibitors drop systemic pressure, not pulmonary.
Beta-blockers reduce the cardiac output she depends on.
No airway disease.
Nitrates act on systemic veins, not PAH.

steps.x: **C. Endothelin receptor antagonist.**

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. Despite anticoagulation, an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE-5 inhibitor, his breathlessness is now present at rest and he has had further syncope. He has no other illness. His pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 98/64 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
